year_start.evidence: No start date for a contemporary relocation found. In 2016 residents were 'just waiting for feedback from government on when the relocation would take place' [para].

households.evidence: The only figure is for all nine Ovalau villages together: 504 households, 2,948 people [para]. No figure for Toki alone.

trigger.evidence: Toki was one of nine Ovalau villages proposed for relocation because they 'were badly affected by the cyclone' (TC Winston, 2016) [para]. McMichael & Katonivualiku (2020) instead frame the study villages as threatened by sea-level rise, so the trigger is ambiguous.

lead.evidence: The iTaukei Affairs Board consulted villagers and the Mineral Resources Department investigated sites [para]. The sources do not say who decided or who implemented.

resident_site_choice.evidence: Village leaders said consultations with the iTaukei Affairs Board had taken place and that residents wanted to move to the hill where the school is [para]. The article does not make clear whether this refers to Toki.

tenure_destination.evidence: Not reported for a contemporary move.

hazard_binding.evidence: The Mineral Resources Department carried out geospatial investigations to identify suitable relocation sites for the nine villages [para]. Whether any site was selected for Toki is not reported.

cases.notes: Barely documented. I could not read the full text of the cited McMichael & Katonivualiku (2020) paper: the PDF uses an undecodable font. Search indexing confirms that Toki is one of its seven study villages, where relocation was 'implemented, initiated or anticipated'. Campbell et al. (APN report, Table 3, citing Nunn 2000) also records an earlier move: 'Naikorokoro, Natokalau, Nukutocia, Rukuruku and Toki on Ovalau I.' moved inland in 1930, about 1 km, onto their own land ('Nearby, own land'), because of coastal erosion. Nunn also reports about 20 m of shoreline retreat at Toki in 65 years. That 1930 move was NOT used for these codes because the sample citation points to the contemporary case. Check which relocation the row intends.

year_start.evidence: Village-level date not found. The move followed the tsunami of 26 December 2004.

households.evidence: Village-level figure not accessible (full text paywalled).

trigger.evidence: "The tsunami that struck the coasts of India on 26 December 2004 resulted in the large-scale destruction of fisher habitations. The post-tsunami rehabilitation effort in Tamil Nadu was directed towards relocating fisher settlements in the interior."

lead.evidence: General context only: in Tamil Nadu, 'NGOs, voluntary organisations and public and private sector enterprises were invited to adopt villages for reconstruction'. The agency for this village is not identified.

resident_site_choice.evidence: The abstract says only that 'participation of fishing communities in house design and in allocation procedures has been limited'. Site choice is not mentioned.

distance.evidence: The sample's place_destination field gives '0.6 km' (presumably taken from Bavinck et al. 2015). Not checked against the full text.

return_to_origin.evidence: "many fishers are actually moving back to their old locations". This finding covers the nine-community sample, not this village specifically.

livelihoods.evidence: "The distance of the new settlements to the shore, however, is regarded as an impediment to engaging in the fishing profession". This is a sample-level finding.

overall.evidence: "many fisher households are satisfied with the quality of the facilities", but distance impedes fishing and fishers move back. This is a sample-level finding.

cases.notes: Full text of Bavinck et al. (2015) is paywalled (Wiley 403; Semantic Scholar lists it as CLOSED). Only the abstract was available. The outcome codes rest on sample-wide abstract findings. They may not hold for a site only 0.6 km away, where the distance-to-shore problem should be weaker. Re-code from the full text if possible.

year_start.evidence: The state of emergency was declared on 11 March 2005 and relocation was then decided. The building site opened in October 2007, the first 40 homes were handed over in February 2011, and the new centre was completed in December 2011 [para].

households.code: 329 people evacuated (of 581 inhabitants); 260-261 houses built for about 560 people
households.evidence: "Sono 124 gli edifici danneggiati, mentre 183 non subiscono danni." Of 581 inhabitants, 329 were evacuated. 260 houses were built for about 560 people [para].

trigger.evidence: The landslide of 6-7 March 2005 partly destroyed the hamlet: "La notte tra il 6 e il 7 marzo 2005 Cavallerizzo è stata colpita da una frana, che ha parzialmente distrutto il borgo."

lead.evidence: Studies commissioned by Civil Protection found that "l'intera frazione di Cavallerizzo è sita su di una frana classificabile come attiva", and total relocation was decided. The citizens' association Cavallerizzo Vive opposed it and demanded recovery of the old village [para].

single_owner.evidence: The Civil Protection Department commissioned the studies, chose Pianette and built all the units. "I 261 edifici realizzati interamente a carico dello Stato" cost about €67.5 million [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: Civil Protection says the project was "concordato con i cittadini" and the houses "sono state personalizzate sulla base delle richieste pervenute ... dai nuclei familiari". A citizens' committee contested relocating elsewhere [para].

tenure_destination.evidence: Tenure of the new homes is not stated. The Council of State later found the new town unlawful for lack of an environmental impact assessment ('new town abusiva'), and the TAR Lazio ordered it legalised after the fact [para]. That legal status may bear on tenure.

hazard_binding.evidence: Pianette was chosen because it offered "condizioni di sicurezza idrogeologica e sismica nettamente migliori".

funding.evidence: The work was done under a state of emergency (declared 11 March 2005, expired 29 February 2012) and was funded 'interamente a carico dello Stato' [para].

distance.evidence: The sample field says 'Pianette (5km)'. Civil Protection describes Pianette as "posta immediatamente ad est del centro abitato di Cerzeto, sul versante opposto", which could be under 5 km.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: No landslide or other hazard event at Pianette is reported. The legal disputes concern the missing environmental impact assessment, not a hazard event [para].

return_to_origin.evidence: A 2021 report says one resident still lives in the old village and another comes back every day to tend a garden and house [para].

livelihoods.evidence: Not documented in the sources I could access. The Guadagno (2014, 2016) texts were not accessible.

overall.evidence: Civil Protection presents it as an example of prevention. Courts found the new town unlawful (no environmental impact assessment); residents were split, and the Cavallerizzo Vive association fought the move [para].

cases.notes: The cited Guadagno chapter on academia.edu returned 403 and was not read. The icalabresi (2021) article says 'Sono venti circa' about the people who moved to the new town, some from neighbouring towns. The context is ambiguous, so it was not used for occupancy. The same article says the old village will become a national firefighter training site. Individuals are not named.

year_start.evidence: Not stated. The move took place before this 2020 note.

households.evidence: "No Parque Juliana, a própria comunidade transferiu cerca de 10 famílias de um setor de risco muito alto (R4) para um onde o risco era menor, dentro da mesma comunidade."

trigger.evidence: Families were moved because of the risk rating (from a very-high-risk R4 sector); some families 'tiveram de ser removidas por causa do risco desta ocorrência' [para]. No specific landslide event is cited for the move.

lead.evidence: "a própria comunidade transferiu cerca de 10 famílias". No government support is mentioned.

single_owner.evidence: The community itself moved the families. No public body is named as responsible [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: The community moved families to a lower-risk sector 'dentro da mesma comunidade'. Those displaced 'encontraram um novo lugar dentro da própria comunidade'.

hazard_binding.evidence: The move was from an R4 (very high) risk sector to 'um onde o risco era menor', which implies use of the municipal R1-R4 risk sectors. No formal site assessment is described.

distance.evidence: The families moved 'dentro da mesma comunidade'.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: The destination is described only as lower-risk ('onde o risco era menor'). 'Todas as comunidades estão localizadas em áreas de risco de deslizamento'. No event at the destination is reported.

overall.evidence: The note gives preliminary findings only, with no evaluation.

cases.notes: The only source is a short research note (4 pp.) based on remote interviews with community leaders during COVID-19. The hazard_at_destination code of exposed_or_hit rests only on the destination being 'lower' risk inside a mapped landslide-risk community. Treat it as weak.

year_start.evidence: Village-level date not found. The move followed the tsunami of 26 December 2004.

trigger.evidence: "The post-tsunami rehabilitation effort in Tamil Nadu was directed towards relocating fisher settlements in the interior."

lead.evidence: General context only: in Tamil Nadu, 'NGOs, voluntary organisations and public and private sector enterprises were invited to adopt villages for reconstruction'.

resident_site_choice.evidence: The abstract reports limited participation in house design and allocation. Site choice is not mentioned.

distance.evidence: The sample field says only '2 sites'.

return_to_origin.evidence: "many fishers are actually moving back to their old locations". This finding covers the nine-community sample.

livelihoods.evidence: "The distance of the new settlements to the shore ... is regarded as an impediment to engaging in the fishing profession". This is a sample-level finding.

overall.evidence: Households were satisfied with facilities, but distance impedes fishing and fishers move back. This is a sample-level finding.

cases.notes: Same limitation as case 34: only the abstract of Bavinck et al. (2015) was available. Outcome codes are sample-level, not specific to this village. I found no other source for this village.

year_start.evidence: APN Table 3 row: 'Helvarg 2000 | Muani, Kadavu | 1997 | <1 | Fiji | R | Nearby, own land | Five houses moved inland | Tropical Cyclone'.

trigger.evidence: The 'Reason for Move' column gives 'Tropical Cyclone'. The table does not say explicitly whether the move followed a specific cyclone.

lead.evidence: Table 3 gives type 'R' (relocation, as opposed to migration or evacuation) but does not say who led it.

tenure_destination.evidence: The 'Boundaries crossed' column gives 'Nearby, own land', i.e. the community's own land.

cases.notes: The only accessible evidence is one row of Campbell, Goldsmith & Koshy's Table 3, which cites Helvarg (2000). Helvarg's E Magazine article was not found online. Separately, recent reporting (e.g. Washington Post, Aug 2025) describes a new, government-approved relocation of the whole village of Muani uphill after seawall failure. That is a different, later relocation and was not coded here.

year_start.evidence: "In 2020, Napakiak developed a groundbreaking 50-year plan – a roadmap for retreating to a new site." Individual structures had been moved from the eroding bank before then.

households.code: 2 families moved by Aug 2023 (2 more planned); 10 house pads funded 2024
households.evidence: "We moved two families from the erosion and we're looking at moving two more before winter." A FEMA grant funds about 10 house pads in the new subdivision [para].

trigger.evidence: GAO lists Napakiak among the 31 Alaska Native villages 'imminently threatened by flooding and erosion'. DGGS: 'Since 1952 ... this section of riverbank has eroded on average 33 to 42 feet per year.'

lead.evidence: "The City of Napakiak, the Native Village of Napakiak, and the Naparyalruar Corporation are all coordinating the retreat." Federal money comes through DOI's Voluntary Community-Driven Relocation Program [para].

single_owner.evidence: Three local entities coordinate the retreat and seek money separately from FEMA, DOI and the Denali Commission. The school district and the state fund the school, and AVCP built the access road [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: The sources do not describe how the site was chosen.

hazard_binding.evidence: DGGS (2021) screened the new school site after construction had begun: "we found no compelling evidence to suggest the new school site will be eroded in the foreseeable future ... the new school will be safe for 150 years."

funding.evidence: $25 million from DOI's Voluntary Community-Driven Relocation Program (2022), about $60 million in state funding for the school, a $2.4 million FEMA grant (2024) and Denali Commission money. Total need is 'upwards of $200 million' [para].

distance.evidence: "As of July 2, 2021, the new school site is located 6000 feet from the Kuskokwim River". The new subdivision is about 2 miles from the river [para].

hazard_at_destination.evidence: The new school opened in 2025, about a mile from the river, and is described as safe from erosion [para].

overall.evidence: The retreat is still under way and only partly funded: 'the federal grant is only a fraction of what is needed' [para].

cases.notes: The cited GAO-09-551 only lists Napakiak among the 31 imminently threatened villages. All process detail comes from later reporting (2021-2025). This is a staged managed retreat within the village area, not a completed relocation.

year_start.evidence: [para] Indexed text of Correa & González (2000): erosion reached 11 m/yr in 1993-97 and 'in 1998 the whole village was moved 200 m landward to a safe location'. Full text not accessed.

households.evidence: Only 'the whole village' and 'a small village of indigenous people' [para].

trigger.evidence: Chronic erosion, worsened after the 1991 earthquake. Non-storm washover 'flooded a small village' so often that it had to be relocated [para].

lead.evidence: [para] Indexed text of Correa & González (2000): 'inhabitants decided to abandon the barrier island and migrate to an interior, ancient beach ridge complex'. I could not check this quote against the full text.

resident_site_choice.evidence: Same indexed passage: the inhabitants decided where to move (the Santa Bárbara beach ridge) [para]. Unchecked.

hazard_binding.evidence: The destination is described as 'a safe location' on an ancient beach ridge. No hazard assessment is described in accessible text.

distance.evidence: Moved about 200 m landward. Figure caption: 'The New Choncho village, relocated inland of his former location, on the Santa Barbara beaches, an ancient barrier.'

overall.evidence: [para] The authors call the move 'a prudent solution which will be the most appropriate for other threatened villages of the Pacific littoral'. This is a judgement on the siting, not on measured outcomes.

cases.notes: IMPORTANT: The Correa & González (2000) case study is the village of El Choncho on the San Juan River delta, Pacific coast (Chocó/Valle). The sample's place name 'San Juan de la Costa' looks like a mislabel of the San Juan delta; verify. The full text is paywalled, and Elsevier withholds the abstract from Crossref and Semantic Scholar. The 1998 date, the 200 m distance and the 'inhabitants decided' passage come from search-indexed text attributed to the paper and could not be read at source.

year_start.evidence: Not accessible (Xu et al. 2020 is paywalled).

households.evidence: Search indexing of the PDD 'Planned Relocation in Asia' snapshot gave two different figures (about 19 people vs 0.25 thousand). I could not open the document to resolve this.

trigger.evidence: The abstract refers to 'unstable landslide risk management in Dabashan Village' [para]. Whether the move followed an event or came before one is unclear.

distance.evidence: The destination is the Songpan county seat (sample field). Distance not stated.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: Not accessible. The abstract warns generally about secondary geological hazards from relocation infrastructure [para].

cases.notes: Barely accessible. Xu et al. (2020) classify Dabashan as an 'urbanization type' relocation community (as opposed to the 'characteristic tourism type'), from the abstract via search. The PDD Asia snapshot lists Dabashan (Songpan County, Aba Prefecture, Sichuan) as a rural-to-urban relocation for landslide hazard, but its PDF could not be parsed. All process and outcome variables are unknown.

year_start.evidence: "The residents of the villages of Fayzobod, Tagnob, Dashtigullo, Kirov, and Turdiyev were resettled to safer areas after the flood of 2005."

households.evidence: No figure for Tagnob or Kondara. National totals only (Table 6: 625 households resettled in 2005).

trigger.evidence: "resettled to safer areas after the flood of 2005"

lead.evidence: Hamadoni is a case study of "Forced migration caused by natural disasters and organized by the state". "Territories for resettlement are chosen by the central authorities at the instruction of district authorities without the involvement of future environmental migrants."

single_owner.evidence: Sites are chosen by central authorities on the instruction of district authorities, and 'Ministries, departments, and local authorities shall implement' the support measures (transport, roads, health, schools, water) [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: "In Hamadoni, 88.5% did not participate in the discussions, whereas 11.5% chose places of residence themselves."

tenure_destination.evidence: "All residents received assistance and land plots, and they built houses." At Kondara 'new houses were built for them'. The type of tenure is not stated.

hazard_binding.evidence: The report says only 'resettled to safer areas'. No site hazard assessment is described.

funding.evidence: Resettlement ran under a national programme for environmental migrants. Each household gets a concessional loan of 3,000 somoni, a 300-somoni lump sum and a plot of 0.08-0.10 ha. The Agency for Social Protection, Employment and Migration recorded 6,643 households resettled in 2000-2010 [para].

distance.evidence: Kondara is described only as 'the new territory'. Distance not stated.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: "they do not feel safe. The annual spring floods of the Siyohob River, the threat of floods along the Panj River, and, above all, a possible break in the Sarez Lake cause the people to consider further resettlement."

return_to_origin.evidence: Some plan to move on, to ancestral land in Shuroobod District or to cities. Return to Tagnob itself is not reported [para].

livelihoods.evidence: "In this village [Kondara], there is no clean water for drinking, no water for irrigation, and no pastures. Hence, it is impossible to live in this area no matter how much one would like to."

overall.evidence: "The majority plan to migrate. Their dream is to leave this village forever."

cases.notes: Tagnob and Kondara are in Hamadoni District, Khatlon Province, not Varzob. Flood of 2005. The Kondara group is 'One group of the environmental migrants, who lost everything'. Other affected households moved higher within the same village. The site-choice figure (88.5% did not take part) is for all Hamadoni respondents.

trigger.evidence: "It presents two historically-grounded, comparative case studies of post-flood resettlement in rural Mozambique."

return_to_origin.evidence: "The ability to secure a viable livelihood was a key determinant of whether resettlers remained in their new locations or returned to the river valleys despite the risks posed by floods." This covers both case studies, not Chicomo specifically.

livelihoods.evidence: "The studies demonstrate a movement away from rain-fed subsistence agriculture towards commercial agriculture and non-agricultural activities." This covers both case studies.

overall.evidence: The abstract gives no overall judgement.

cases.notes: Arnall et al. (2013) is paywalled (Wiley 403; the CentAUR repository was blocked by an anti-bot page). Only the abstract was used. I could not confirm which of the two case studies is Chicomo or which flood (1977 vs 2000) it concerns. Re-code from the full text.

year_start.evidence: Residents asked for help in 2006. The village relocated in January 2014 (a government-supported project from 2012) [para].

households.evidence: The original village had "26 houses in which 32 families lived". "30 identical houses were built in accordance with the villagers' choices".

trigger.evidence: Residents 'approached government officials to request relocation assistance' after 'coastal and river flooding, erosion, sea-level rise, and increasing wave intensity' [para].

lead.evidence: "In 2006, Vunidogoloa's residents approached the Government of Fiji seeking financial assistance for relocation." Also: "The government of Fiji largely organized the Vunidogola relocation as an integrated action across different government ministries."

single_owner.evidence: "Many ministries and donor agencies (e.g., International Labour Organization) contributed funding and resources." It was organised 'as an integrated action across different government ministries'.

resident_site_choice.evidence: The new site lies within the community's own mataqali land, and houses were built 'in accordance with the villagers' choices'. The sources I read do not describe how the site itself was chosen.

tenure_destination.evidence: "The new site is located within mataqali (clan) ancestral land."

hazard_binding.evidence: No geotechnical or hazard assessment of Kenani is reported in the sources consulted.

funding.evidence: "the Fijian government paid approx. 740,000 USD, and the community paid out approx. 240,000 USD". The sources do not say whether this came from a standing programme or an ad hoc allocation.

distance.evidence: "about 1 km directly inland (or 2 km by road)"

hazard_at_destination.evidence: At the new site, residents report more exposure to cyclones (TC Yasa, 2020: 'we are more exposed'). Unfinished drainage risks erosion: 'Inadequate drainage could lead to further erosion at the new site.'

return_to_origin.evidence: "While the new site is on mataqali land, and many people continue to visit the old site for fishing and farming."

livelihoods.evidence: Livelihood initiatives 'faltered and failed over time': pineapple plantations stopped by 2016 and fish ponds became 'non-operational after a few years'. 'Access to the ocean, fishing grounds, and coastal food sources has reduced.'

overall.evidence: "Community relocation can lead to adverse consequences for wellbeing, even with community participation and extensive funding". The move is widely praised as a success story, but outcomes 'evolve over time' [para].

cases.notes: The sample's hazard field says 'flood', but the sources describe combined coastal erosion, inundation and sea-level rise. Early accounts (2015-2019) report livelihoods re-established through fish ponds and pineapples, while the 2024 longitudinal study reports these failed. I coded livelihoods from the later study. A Sept 2026 report says the community spent about FJD 600,000 of its own money, and that drainage and farm roads remain unfinished.

trigger.evidence: "In 2013, Typhoon Haiyan decimated informal settlements in Tacloban City's coastline. In response, the government elected to relocate thousands of households to a previously undeveloped section of the city, Tacloban North."

lead.evidence: Tacloban North sites range 'from small non-governmental sites to large-scale National Housing Authority sites'. The developer of Hitunlob was not found.

overall.evidence: Palagi & Javernick-Will (2020) report that 'fast construction, full occupancy, and close proximity to an economic and administrative center' were necessary for livability. No site-level result for Hitunlob was accessible.

cases.notes: 'Hitunlob' does not appear in the 2018 GPO survey of 13 Tacloban sites (GMA Kapuso, Guadalupe, Habitat 4428, Lion's Village, New Hope, North Hill, Operation Blessing, Ridgeview, SM Cares, St. Francis, UNDP, Diana Villa, and others). Web searches found no mention of it. The MDPI and ASCE papers cited in the sample could not be fetched (403). The name may be misspelled; check it against the Palagi & Javernick-Will site tables.

year_start.evidence: The groundbreaking for 1,750 houses at the 'government-owned 10-hectare Indahag Relocation Site' was on 10 February 2012. House-and-lot certificates were awarded on 28 September 2012 [para].

households.code: 1,750 houses planned; one batch of 200 families awarded house and lot (Sept 2012)
households.evidence: The groundbreaking was for '1,750 houses'. The award ceremony headline reads '200 Families Get Houses & Lots'.

trigger.evidence: The site is for survivors of Typhoon Washi (Sendong), December 2011: 'Sendong survivors from various barangays received certificates' [para].

lead.evidence: Construction was undertaken by "Habitat for Humanity – Philippines" on a government-owned site, with NHA, DSWD and the city involved [para]. Santiago et al. (2018) describe the three Washi sites as managed by the city government, the NHA regional office and an academic institution, but I could not confirm which one is Indahag.

single_owner.evidence: Government land, Habitat construction, NHA and DSWD participation, and the Mayor and council distributing certificates [para].

tenure_destination.evidence: Survivors received certificates at an 'Awarding of House and Lot Ceremony' assigning them permanent homes [para]. These are award certificates; no title is mentioned.

hazard_binding.evidence: No geohazard screening is reported in the sources consulted.

livelihoods.evidence: "No one is looking after us – the people here have no livelihood" (a resettlement board director, Dec 2013). Small livelihood projects were short-lived. Water had been trucked in, then the deliveries stopped.

overall.evidence: Santiago et al. (2018): survivors 'still suffer from the effects of privation and displacement more than two years after the disaster', and the three agency-driven sites had 'disparate outcomes' [para]. This is not specific to Indahag.

cases.notes: Santiago et al. (2018) is paywalled; the Ateneo archive and academia.edu returned 403. Indahag is in Cagayan de Oro and has Habitat Phase 1 and 2. Do not confuse it with the '722 Relocation' site built from 2018. Individuals are not named.

cases.place_destination: Nueva Choluteca (two relocation sites - 1 government, one community)

year_start.evidence: "Since January 1999, when this 117 hectares of land in Nueva Choluteca was confirmed as the reconstruction site, OIM ... has built approximately 850 temporary shelters"

households.code: 2,154 housing lots allocated (about 1,300 permanent units existing at time of study)
households.evidence: "This project allocated 2,154 housing lots". Most of 'the 1,300 existing units' were concrete block with zinc roofs.

trigger.evidence: Hurricane Mitch hit Choluteca between 25 October and 2 November 1998. OIM sheltered 'families who are waiting for the completion of their permanent houses'.

lead.evidence: Houses were built by many NGOs and donors (Atlas Logistics 'over 250 housing units', CECI, Samaritan's Purse, the Spanish Consulate, the Catholic Church and others). "The 'laid back' attitude of the government amidst of the flurry of reconstruction efforts by international NGOs in Nueva Choluteca".

single_owner.evidence: Local municipalities played 'an important role in the procurement and allotment of the land' and helped NGOs select families. Each NGO built to a common 10 x 20 m lot rule, and more than 20 organisations are listed [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: The report does not describe residents taking part in site choice.

tenure_destination.evidence: Land came from Banco Occidente and was allotted via the municipality [para]. The tenure of recipients is not stated.

hazard_binding.evidence: The site 'was thought ideal for relocation, first, because a single-owned, large acreage of land is hard to obtain in Choluteca ... and second because the land is relatively flat ground, naturally protected by a barricade of mountains on three sides.' No hazard assessment is described.

funding.evidence: Funded by NGO and donor reconstruction money (e.g. CECI had financial responsibility for its 52 units, which Atlas Logistics built) [para].

distance.evidence: "Located 15 kilometers from central Choluteca". The land 'was located eight kilometers from the old city'.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: No hazard event at the site is reported. The report recommends stormwater drainage.

livelihoods.evidence: "most families cite water supply and employment opportunities as burning issues". The report gives no comparison with livelihoods before the move.

overall.evidence: Residents 'almost unanimously agree that the standard and quality of housing provided in this community is far better that what they previously had', but water, sewage, electricity and employment were lacking.

cases.notes: The cited Zhang (2016) was not accessible. Coding relies on a c.1999-2000 McGill/Natural Hazards Center field report on Nueva Choluteca (Limón de la Cerca), an early-stage snapshot. I could not verify the sample's description of 'two relocation sites - 1 government, one community'. Alaniz's later work compares two NGO-built Mitch resettlements with very different social outcomes, but I did not confirm whether one of them is Nueva Choluteca.

year_start.evidence: "Guédiawaye : 109 familles victimes d'inondations relogées au Plan Jaxaay (Le Soleil, jeudi 11 mars 2010)". The plan itself was launched after the 2005 floods.

households.code: 109 families (part of 1,800 families registered from Wakhinane-Nimzatt and Médina Gounass)
households.evidence: "Quelque 109 familles de la commune d'arrondissement de Wakhinane Nimzatt ... ont rejoint jeudi leurs nouvelles maisons sur le site du Plan Jaxaay". "ces 109 familles font partie des 1.800 autres familles victimes d'inondations ... recensées pour bénéficier des nouveaux logements".

trigger.evidence: "nous déplaçons ces familles qui habitaient dans des zones inondées pour les reloger sur ce site (Cité Jaxaay)"

lead.evidence: "... pour les reloger sur ce site (Cité Jaxaay) conformément à la volonté du président de la République". Whole sectors 'ont d'ailleurs été déplacés, dans le cadre de programmes gouvernementaux'.

single_owner.evidence: A dedicated 'Projet Plan Jaxaay' had its own coordination (a deputy coordinator is quoted). Search summaries say the State worked with SN-HLM to expropriate the site, which I did not verify. Drainage and sanitation, due before occupation, were never finished [para].

resident_site_choice.evidence: Families were 'recensées pour bénéficier'. Their say in the site is not described.

tenure_destination.evidence: The housing arrangement (ownership vs rent-to-own) is not stated in the sources consulted.

hazard_binding.evidence: The plan lacked 'études d'impacts sérieusement du site en amont'; the relocation site was itself flood-prone [para].

funding.evidence: A special presidential plan with '52 milliards de francs CFA pour la construction de 4.000 logements sociaux'. Work stopped in 2014 [para].

distance.evidence: The site is in the Kounoune-Niacourab / Keur Massar area. Distance from Wakhinane-Nimzatt is not stated.

hazard_at_destination.evidence: "Jaxaay-Parcelles est devenue un véritable réceptacle des eaux." "Pratiquement, toutes les entrées de la commune sont impactées par les eaux stagnantes durant toute l'année."

overall.evidence: A resident: "Le Plan Jaxaay est un échec!" The article frames it as a paradox: housing meant to remove flood victims from flooding was built in a flood-prone place, and 'la stagnation des eaux demeure une réalité'.

cases.notes: The Vollmer (2009) EPFL thesis was not consulted. The GRDR monograph reproduces an APS/Le Soleil dispatch of 11 March 2010 on the move of the 109 families. The plan dates from 2005-06; first units were delivered in late 2006 or early 2007, and work stopped in 2014. Outcome evidence is from the whole Jaxaay site (2026 press), not only the Wakhinane-Nimzatt families.
